stem: A child has bilious vomiting, abdominal distension and guarding, and bowel obstruction is suspected; what is the best next-step plan?

options.text: Arrange an AXR, keep the child fasted, insert an NGT, and seek early surgical review
Arrange a CXR because pneumonia is the preferred explanation
Rely on ultrasound because AXR has no role when obstruction is suspected
Encourage oral intake while waiting because surgical referral can be delayed
Avoid analgesia until the diagnosis is certain

explanation: Arrange an AXR, keep the child fasted, insert an NGT, and seek early surgical review. This is the appropriate next-step plan when bowel obstruction is suspected, with bilious vomiting, distension and guarding suggesting surgical pathology.

rationale: Bilious vomiting, distension and guarding are red flags for surgical pathology. AXR is recommended when obstruction is suspected, and bowel obstruction management includes fasting, NGT decompression and early surgical review.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because suspected bowel obstruction should be managed with AXR, fasting, NGT decompression and early surgical review.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because a CXR does not address suspected bowel obstruction and pneumonia is not the preferred explanation here.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because AXR still has a role when obstruction is suspected; ultrasound is not the sole test.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because the child should be kept fasted and reviewed early by surgery rather than given oral intake.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because analgesia should not be withheld; appropriate pain relief is recommended.
